How we ran this comparison

Same rows, different methods

The conventional models used training-only preprocessing and repeated stratified cross-validation for a modest hyperparameter search. TabICLv2 used the official checkpoint, one ensemble member, and no task-specific fine-tuning. Their compute budgets differ.

Interpreting uncertainty

Intervals condition on the fitted model and observed test class counts; they do not include training variability or test paired differences. Batch timings are hardware-dependent; TabICLv2 preprocessing time is excluded.

What is not measured: temporal or cross-organization transfer, fairness, causal effects, and operational outcomes. The test sets have been inspected and must not be reused for model selection.

A defensible P&L bridge

Culture does not enter the income statement directly. Its effects travel through work.

Work conditionsClarity, trust, learning time, manager support
BehaviorAdoption, coordination, voice, internal movement
OperationsCycle time, quality, capacity, absence, regretted exits
EconomicsRevenue enabled, avoided rework, hiring and risk cost
P&L evidenceIncremental margin after technology, change and control costs

Do not multiply correlations into ROI. Prespecify the operational pathway, use a credible comparison group or phased rollout, include implementation cost, and report uncertainty and distributional effects. Consolidated culture can support coordination; enforced uniformity can suppress dissent and increase risk.

Imagine a bank trying to make development easier to access. The goal: build organizational capability while giving people a fair, voluntary opportunity to grow.

See more areas of potential impact

Workforce planning

Potential contributionUse aggregate demand and capacity trends to test staffing scenarios and service resilience. Evaluate forecasts with time-based holdouts; do not treat projections as a directive to reduce a particular team.

Hiring & access

Potential contributionAudit aggregate recruiting funnel accessibility and process time across lawful groups. An audit is different from ranking applicants; it can identify a process to investigate, not prove discrimination on its own.

Learning & mobility

Potential contributionUnderstand access to learning time, information and internal opportunities; compare voluntary program outcomes with a credible evaluation design. Uptake alone does not demonstrate benefit.

Employee experience

Potential contributionCombine sufficiently aggregated, validated employee feedback with workload and work-design context. Protect confidentiality and test whether response rates or survey design bias the results.

Equity & retention

Potential contributionReview aggregate opportunity, compensation patterns and observed exits, where lawful and supported by appropriate denominators. Investigate context and uncertainty; do not infer individual intent or prescribe individual employment actions.

These are possible applications and outcomes, not claims that JPMorganChase has deployed them or that they will produce a particular effect. Public data do not establish impact at the bank.

Explore the proposed study design
01

Define the question with employees

Prespecify eligible groups, job families, geography and period. Ask whether an inclusive offer of career information and protected learning time improves access and experience. Consult employees and representatives before deciding what to collect.

02

Evaluate the offer, not the person

If feasible and approved, compare randomized business units receiving a voluntary offer now with a later rollout. Account for clustered units and spillovers. If randomization is not feasible, explain the selection bias and assumptions of any observational comparison.

03

Measure both sides of the relationship

Track aggregate access, voluntary uptake, internal applications and transfers, staff coverage, and employee-reported opportunity and workload. Specify denominators and timing. An application is not proof of motivation or an intervention effect.

04

Decide with safeguards

Review uncertainty, negative results, distributional effects where lawful, disclosure risk, access controls and the employee experience. Small-cell and complementary suppression must be designed for the actual data and releases. Do not rank individuals for employment decisions.

What the current experiments can say. The public TabArena task is job-change intention; the IBM sample is fictional. Neither validates this proposal, estimates an effect in a bank, or supports conclusions about JPMorganChase employees.

The datasetsSee what the models were trained and tested on.

Psychology gives us concepts—like engagement, fairness, and psychological safety. Analytics requires us to define how those concepts are measured. A field in a table is not automatically a valid measure of a person's motivation or well-being.

To explore one narrow predictive question, we compare conventional methods with a pretrained tabular foundation model on two separately sourced datasets. They have different targets and cannot be treated as a cross-organizational transfer test.

Dataset 01 · TabArena

Job-change intention

A dataset of 19,158 records curated for TabArena. Our CPU-bounded experiment uses a fixed stratified sample of 1,500 rows. The target is whether a participant is looking for a job change—not whether they actually leave an employer.

Read the OpenML dataset card ↗
Dataset 02 · Fictional

IBM attrition sample

A fictional, undated demonstration dataset of 1,470 records. It is useful for checking methods, but its patterns are not observations of IBM's workforce or an operational HR benchmark.

Read the IBM dataset source ↗

The history of workTrace the ideas behind people analytics.

The story of human resources is not a straight line from personnel files to predictive models. It is a conversation about how work is organized, how people experience it, and who gets to decide what counts.

Industrialization made the administration of work more formal. Applied psychology brought attention to learning, motivation, selection, and fatigue. Labor movements and standards demanded that working conditions and rights be part of the story. Later, organizational research examined the social and psychological contexts in which work happens.

Analytics inherits all of these histories. A data point can tell us something useful, but it can also leave out power, context, and the person behind the record.

A useful model begins with a useful question—and a clear understanding of what the data can actually represent.
A selective chronology

Explore the milestones

Open a period to read more

Before 1800Before industrial HR

Work was organized through households, agriculture, craft, trade, armies and public administration, with apprenticeship, obligations, hierarchy and coercion varying across societies. These arrangements are antecedents to workforce coordination, not a single origin of modern HR.

Psychology & workLearning, belonging, authority and fairness already mattered, even though modern organizational psychology did not yet exist.

Measurement & analyticsRecords, wages and production counts are early forms of administration; surviving records tell us more about institutions than individual experience.

Source: ILO historical context ↗
1800–1890sIndustrialization & labor organization

Factory growth made hiring, wages, working time, safety and discipline recurring organizational problems. Workers organized collectively, while reforms and welfare practices developed unevenly.

Psychology & workFatigue, skill and the lived effects of work entered public debate alongside power, inequality and collective voice.

Measurement & analyticsPayroll and headcounts made labor visible in administrative records, but what was counted reflected employers’ priorities.

Source: ILO history ↗
1890s–1910sEfficiency & early applied psychology

Scientific management and time-and-motion studies sought to organize tasks and standardize work. Early industrial psychologists applied experimental methods to selection and work.

Psychology & workAttention, aptitude, fatigue and human differences became subjects of systematic study. Efficiency-oriented methods could overlook autonomy and workers’ knowledge.

Measurement & analyticsTiming tasks and assessing job requirements linked measurement to management. Measures need job relevance, reliability and fairness.

Source: History of industrial-organizational psychology ↗
1910s–1920sWar, testing & labor standards

World War I accelerated testing, classification and training in several countries. The ILO was created in 1919; its first conference addressed working time and other labor standards.

Psychology & workAssessment and classification grew, but early tests were also shaped by language, cultural assumptions and discriminatory institutions.

Measurement & analyticsLarge-scale scores and personnel records enabled comparison; validity and the consequences of classification must be examined rather than assumed.

Source: ILO original records ↗
1920s–1930sHuman relations & the Hawthorne studies

Research at Western Electric helped direct attention to social relations and working conditions, influencing the human-relations movement.

Psychology & workInformal groups, supervision and worker attitudes became central themes, though these ideas should not erase conflict, pay or material conditions.

Measurement & analyticsThe studies became a lesson about observing work. Later analysis challenged popular accounts of the illumination results; observation alone does not establish causality.

Source: Levitt & List, 2011 ↗
1940s–1950sPersonnel, training & human factors

World War II expanded applied work on selection, training and equipment. Formal personnel functions and postwar research into work attitudes grew.

Psychology & workMotivation, job satisfaction, learning and human-machine interaction joined aptitude and selection. Their measurement involves constructs, not directly observable facts.

Measurement & analyticsJob analysis, tests and surveys connected psychological theory with structured measurement; assessment quality depends on context.

Source: Oxford history ↗
1950s–1960sMotivation, groups & organization

Researchers developed theories of motivation, leadership and group behavior; organizational development drew on group dynamics. In the US, Title VII of the 1964 Civil Rights Act addressed employment discrimination.

Psychology & workNeeds, expectations, leadership and group processes offered competing explanations; no single theory fits every worker or context.

Measurement & analyticsSurveys and statistical associations became common, while employment discrimination raised questions about whose outcomes and opportunities were being measured.

Source: EEOC historical overview ↗
1970s–1980sWork design, rights & organizational behavior

Industrial psychology broadened into industrial-organizational psychology; job design, worker participation and the social context of organizations received greater attention. Personnel management increasingly connected with business strategy.

Psychology & workAutonomy, feedback, meaningful work, commitment and stress helped shift attention from individual traits to the design of work.

Measurement & analyticsQuestionnaires and administrative systems made larger studies possible, but measures of attitudes require reliability, construct validity and attention to unequal power.

Source: Oxford history ↗
1990sEngagement, safety & strategic HR

Strategic HRM and organizational behavior grew alongside research on engagement and team learning. Kahn studied psychological conditions for engagement; Edmondson studied team psychological safety.

Psychology & workMeaningfulness, safety and availability are concepts in Kahn’s qualitative work; psychological safety is a shared team belief, not something to infer from a single personnel field.

Measurement & analyticsSurvey research and multilevel analysis can examine individuals and teams, but cross-sectional relationships do not by themselves prove interventions work.

Source: Edmondson, 1999 ↗
2000sEvidence synthesis & digital HR

HR information systems and online workflows expanded; systematic reviews and meta-analyses brought findings across studies together.

Psychology & workOrganizational justice and the job demands–resources model connected fairness, work conditions and well-being to organizational outcomes.

Measurement & analyticsMeta-analysis, surveys and longitudinal methods provide different kinds of evidence. Digital traces are not direct measurements of emotions or intentions.

Source: Colquitt et al., 2001 ↗
2010sPeople analytics & predictive models

People analytics grew as organizations combined HR data, statistics and machine learning; a scoping review noted differing definitions and employer-centered value propositions.

Psychology & workTurnover, engagement, learning and team research require theories of context, voice, motivation and fairness—not just a target label.

Measurement & analyticsRegression and predictive ML enable pattern finding, but leakage, missing outcomes, proxy discrimination and surveillance can make a model misleading or harmful.

Source: People analytics scoping review ↗
2020–2026Foundation models & responsible research

Foundation models pretrained on many synthetic tabular tasks now compete on general tabular benchmarks. Their published performance does not establish value in workforce settings.

Psychology & workHuman experience, social structure and institutional context are not automatically captured by a vector representation. Employee voice and worker rights remain essential.

Measurement & analyticsA defensible evaluation needs prospective data, measured constructs, external and temporal tests, uncertainty, privacy protection and comparisons to strong baselines. PeopleFM has no workforce results yet.

Source: TabICLv2, ICML 2026 ↗
A note on scope. These overlapping chapters are a selected narrative with a US and European emphasis, not an exhaustive global history. The original data behind historical studies are not all public or comparable. The experiments below do not recreate those studies.
Why HR mattersUnderstand its value to people and organizations.

Work brings people with different needs, skills, and responsibilities into a shared institution. Someone must help make the rules of that relationship visible, workable, and accountable.

Human resource management is the collection of policies and practices through which organizations coordinate that relationship: defining roles, recruiting and developing people, administering pay and benefits, supporting safe work, handling concerns, and helping managers apply workplace policies. Some of this work belongs to managers, worker representatives, and other teams as well as HR; a department name alone does not guarantee that it is done well.

For an organization, the work can support continuity and coordination. Hiring and development help build capabilities; clear responsibilities, feedback, and fair procedures can help people work together; attention to safety and employment obligations can reduce avoidable harm and disruption. A 2026 cross-national meta-analysis examines how investment in practices such as training, participation, and job design relates to firm performance—and why national context matters. Such associations do not prove that a particular policy will improve every firm.

For a person at work, HR can affect much more than an administrative transaction. It can shape access to development, the clarity of expectations, pay and benefits, the ability to raise concerns, and the conditions under which work is done. Research on organizational justice distinguishes fairness of outcomes from fairness of procedures and interpersonal treatment; these are related to how people experience their workplace.

Those two perspectives can overlap, but they do not always align. A policy aimed at productivity can also intensify work; a formal channel for feedback is useful only if people can speak without fear of retaliation and are heard. A 2025 systematic review describes positive links between HR practices and outcomes such as engagement, alongside risks including exhaustion. Its findings do not establish a universal causal recipe.

For the organization

Build the conditions for work

Coordinate skills, roles, development, continuity, and workplace processes. Measure whether practices are effective in context rather than assuming that a policy works because it exists.

For the person

Make work more accountable

Support fair treatment, opportunities to learn, safer conditions, clear expectations, and channels for voice. These are meaningful outcomes in their own right, not merely inputs to performance.

Good people research asks both what helps an organization function and what makes work fair, safe, and worthwhile for the people doing it.
A research boundary. HR can facilitate these outcomes, but responsibility is shared with leadership, managers, workers, and worker representatives. Research findings are often context-dependent; associations and organizational claims should not be treated as proof of causality.
Inside the modelSee how TabICLv2 works.

Instead of learning a new set of model weights for each table, a tabular foundation model is pretrained across many tasks. At inference, labeled training examples form a context for predicting unseen rows. The research question is whether that prior experience helps on a new task.

TabICLv2's published classification architecture processes the table in three stages. Our experiment uses its official checkpoint; it does not create a newly pretrained PeopleFM model.

01

Read down each column

A column-wise set transformer uses induced attention and target-aware embeddings. The paper describes three blocks with 128 inducing vectors, dimension 128, and eight attention heads.

02

Combine features within a row

A three-layer row transformer uses four learned CLS tokens. Their outputs are concatenated into a 512-dimensional representation for each row.

03

Learn from the context

A 12-layer in-context transformer lets test rows attend to labeled training rows. A prediction head produces the output; held-out test labels are never supplied as context.

features + training labels → column embeddings → row representations → contextual prediction

This is a conceptual summary, not a complete implementation. The paper also describes synthetic task generation and attention changes for long-context generalization. See the architecture and appendix in the TabICLv2 paper for the full specification.

The foundation-model frontierExplore current research and emerging companies.

The next question is not simply whether a larger model scores better. It is whether the model is suited to the kind of question we are asking—and whether the evidence supports using it in a human setting.

Tabular, time-series and world-action models work with different kinds of context. Each opens a different research path. The examples below are proposals for offline HR research, not validated PeopleFM capabilities.

01 / Tables

Learn from structured context

Tabular models condition on labeled examples to predict a table's outcome. Potential research: compare aggregate workforce patterns under scarce labels, with strong baselines and careful leakage checks.

02 / Time

Forecast a changing system

Time-series models forecast future values from ordered observations. Potential research: aggregate training demand or staffing flows, using rolling time-based evaluation and realistic uncertainty.

03 / Actions

Model states and actions

World-action research often concerns physical robot behavior and predicted scene evolution. A workforce-planning simulator is a separate, unvalidated idea—not an established application of these robots.

The distinction matters. A forecast predicts what may happen under observed patterns. A causal study asks what would change under an intervention. A generated scenario is neither proof of a forecast nor proof of a causal effect. None of these paths should automate individual employment decisions.

From concepts to measuresConnect psychology to responsible research.

Good people analytics begins with a clear construct, a question shaped with workers, and a measure that is appropriate for the context. A number is useful only when we know what it represents.

The table below connects established concepts in work psychology and HR to possible aggregate research measures. It is a map for designing studies—not a way to diagnose or score people.

Opportunity & mobility

Question. Can people see and pursue opportunities that fit their goals?

Study. Examine eligible populations, voluntary applications and transfers; combine aggregate patterns with employee feedback. An application is not a measure of ability or a preference to leave.

Learning & growth

Question. Is development accessible, useful and supported by time and management?

Study. Consider access, voluntary participation, protected learning time and feedback. Selection into training can make simple before-and-after comparisons misleading.

Engagement & safety

Question. Do people find their work meaningful and feel able to speak up?

Study. Use validated, appropriately aggregated surveys and qualitative feedback. Kahn's engagement research and Edmondson's team research concern distinct constructs; a digital trace cannot stand in for either automatically.

Fairness & voice

Question. Are outcomes, procedures and interpersonal treatment experienced as fair?

Study. Examine the multiple dimensions of organizational justice and protect channels for speaking up. A statistical parity metric alone does not capture the whole experience of fairness.

Work design & well-being

Question. Are demands, resources and safety conditions appropriate?

Study. Pair validated measures and worker feedback with context such as workload and support. Overtime or another single field is not a diagnosis of burnout; evidence and effects vary by context.

Measurement matters. Each measure needs a defined population, time window, denominator and level of analysis. Review bias, consent or other lawful basis, privacy, and whether the measure is valid for each context.
What the results cannot tell usUnderstand the boundaries of prediction.

Even a well-calibrated model cannot tell us why a person feels a particular way, whether an intervention will help, or how an organization should treat an individual. Those questions require appropriate psychological measurement, worker participation, causal designs, and governance.

Excluding a sensitive attribute from training does not remove its proxies. Small groups, undated features, and unknown data collection processes introduce additional uncertainty. PeopleFM is intended for offline research and aggregate analysis; it is not designed for individual hiring, promotion, compensation, termination, or disciplinary recommendations.

The strength of this research will be measured by the evidence it can withstand, including negative results.
Reproduce the researchAccess executable code and aggregate results.

The research bundle includes the executable benchmark, dataset preparation scripts, an aggregate audit and the tests. Download the public datasets separately after reviewing their source terms. The example below audits the fictional IBM sample and runs the same conventional benchmark described above.

python -m pip install -e .
python experiments/audit_dataset.py \
  --file datasets/raw/ibm.csv --target Attrition \
  --min-group 20 --output results/ibm/aggregate_audit.json
python -m peoplefm.benchmarks.run --config configs/benchmark.json
Download executable research bundle

Run from the extracted project folder with Python 3.10 or later. Place the public IBM CSV at datasets/raw/ibm.csv; the bundle's README describes the TabArena preparation and optional model dependencies. The audit writes counts and a checksum—not employee rankings. A small target class causes the entire target distribution to be suppressed to prevent simple subtraction.

To rerun the TabArena comparison, install the optional packages and download the OpenML ARFF source to datasets/raw/jobchange.arff. The pretrained checkpoint downloads on first use. XGBoost and LightGBM may require the platform's OpenMP runtime. The fixed sample and single split are not the official TabArena folds.

python -m pip install -r requirements-benchmark.txt
# Obtain OpenML dataset 46935 as datasets/raw/jobchange.arff first.
python experiments/prepare_tabarena.py
python -m peoplefm.benchmarks.run --config configs/jobchange.json
python experiments/tabicl_compare.py --config configs/jobchange.json

These are offline research scripts. Before using real employee records, secure appropriate authorization and data protections; aggregate output and suppression alone do not guarantee anonymity.
